clue.text: Fumble about university, emptying it of camp gear

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is wrapped around another

parts.note: to fumble is to grope clumsily

indicators.note: to empty a word is to take out its insides, leaving only the shell of first and last letters

parts.note: the word with its middle removed

explanation.surface: Someone fumbles drunkenly round a university campus, then tidies away their camping kit.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'it' in 'emptying it' points back to university, not to anything new, so only its outside letters survive.
explanation.definitionFit: A tent is pegged down by tensioned lines, which are standard equipment when pitching camp outdoors.

clue.text: Out of tune, quality is not the same

indicators.note: something taken out of a phrase is drawn from inside its run of letters

parts.note: read straight through the two words, ignoring the comma

explanation.surface: A singer is told that being out of tune makes the quality of the performance uneven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of tune' reads as a musical phrase, but 'Out of' is the signal and the letters run across tune and quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that differ in size, amount or value are described this way, a plain synonym for differing.

clue.text: Concerned with evil sticky stuff

parts.note: re means concerning, as in the heading of a letter
sin is wickedness

explanation.surface: Someone is worried about wicked, gooey substances.
explanation.walkthrough: RE is the Latin-derived 'in the matter of' used in memos; it is a common crossword gift for 'about' or 'concerning'.
explanation.definitionFit: Trees exude a thick gummy sap that hardens, which is the natural substance meant by this tacky material.

clue.text: Paint FBI agents into a hole

indicators.note: putting something into a space places it inside that space

parts.note: a pit is a hole in the ground; the article just sets it up
G-men is American slang for FBI agents, short for Government men

explanation.surface: An order to daub the federal agents and push them into a hole, like a gangster film.
explanation.walkthrough: G-men is 1930s American slang for Federal Bureau of Investigation agents. The noun 'Paint' looks like a verb in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Colouring matter is the substance that gives a coat its hue, so the noun stands in for colouring material.

clue.text: A tax U-turn if shoddily managed leads into regression

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a U-turn sends a vehicle back the way it came, so letters run backwards

parts.note: VAT is value added tax, the British sales tax

indicators.note: the leaders of words are the letters at their front

parts.note: the opening letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A government's tax reversal, handled badly, sends the economy backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'U-turn' reads as a political climbdown but simply turns VAT around. VAT is value added tax, the British equivalent of a sales tax.
explanation.definitionFit: A reversion to ancestral traits or earlier behaviour is a going backwards, so the biological term matches regression.

clue.text: Make disapproving sounds, including 'eff off' and 'sit on this'?

definitions.note: a cryptic pointer to the thing sat on, standing for a noun

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it within, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: tut is the clicking noise of disapproval

indicators.note: something off has gone wrong or bad, so the letters are spoiled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written: the spelt-out name of the letter

explanation.surface: Someone tuts at rude language, telling a person to eff off and sit on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eff off' looks like a mild swear, but 'off' rearranges EFF. The definition recalls Little Miss Muffet, who sat on a tuffet in the nursery rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: A low seat or footstool is what the nursery rhyme heroine perched upon, so the rude invitation describes a stool.

clue.text: Troubled relatives able to change

indicators.note: something troubled is disturbed and unsettled, so the letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A family in difficulty is capable of turning itself around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Troubled relatives' reads as a family drama; the nine letters of relatives are simply reshuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Adaptable people or tools turn readily to many uses, which is the sense of being flexible and adjustable.

clue.text: European slob last to bathe

parts.note: a sloven is an untidy, lazy person

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter only

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A grubby continental is the last one to get washed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last to bathe' sounds like the slob being slow to wash, but it only supplies the final E.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Slovenia is a citizen of a country in central Europe, so a national of that state.

clue.text: Hairstyle on Lucy sure to get ruffled as it's done

parts.note: a bob is a short haircut

indicators.note: ruffled hair is messed up, so these letters are tousled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A hairdresser gives Lucy a bob and tousles it to finish the cut.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface stays in the salon, with 'ruffled' fitting hair. The answer is a British catchphrase meaning 'and there you are', said when a simple task is finished.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom announces that something is complete and easy, much like saying the job is finished, simple as that.

clue.text: Some of these are electric rockers

definitions.meaning: first meaning: fish, some species of which give electric shocks
second meaning: an American rock band of that name

explanation.walkthrough: 'electric rockers' suggests guitar bands, which is half right; the first half points at the fish that stun prey with a charge.
explanation.definitionFit: The electric eel is a famous shocking fish, and the band led by Mark Oliver Everett also takes this name.

clue.text: Healthy food ruined in bloody university

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: gory means covered in blood

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked, so its letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
OU is the Open University, Britain's distance-learning university

explanation.surface: Healthy eating gets wrecked at a university that the speaker damns as bloody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloody' reads as a British swear word, but it means GORY here. The Open University is a UK institution teaching by correspondence.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that is wholesome and beneficial is described with this everyday phrase, so it matches the adjective.

clue.text: Religious person must embrace a church's subtlety

indicators.note: an embrace wraps arms around someone, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: a nun is a woman in a religious order
taken as written
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A devout person is urged to accept the finer points of church teaching.
explanation.walkthrough: CE, the Church of England, is a standard crossword abbreviation for church. The 's is read as 'has', linking wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A fine shade of meaning or slight difference in tone is exactly what a delicacy or refinement amounts to.

clue.text: Go to these text locations to find leaks

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an instruction in a book to look at certain numbered places, split as two words
second meaning: slow escapes of liquid

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a book's cross-reference, 'see pages ...', run together as one word to make the plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Water oozing slowly through walls or soil produces small escapes of fluid, the plural noun for drips.

clue.text: Smelling loo, in fact revolting

indicators.note: revolting can mean rising up against order, so the letters overturn their arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The toilet stinks; in fact it is disgusting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolting' fits a smelly toilet as disgusting, but it is the signal to rebel against the letter order. A loo is a British toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: The scientific name for the sense of scent is the noun matching the act of sniffing, a gerund used as noun.

clue.text: Charlie wearing extra habit

indicators.note: a wearer has clothing around them, so one piece is dressed in another

parts.note: an addition is something extra
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A man called Charlie wears an extra religious robe, like a monk's garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'habit' suggests a monk's robe beside 'wearing', but it means a dependency. Charlie is also slang for cocaine, which deepens the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A compulsive dependence, as on a drug, is commonly called a habit in everyday speech, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: It'd be silly to get this plumbing fixture

indicators.note: silly means foolish or muddled, so the letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone says it would be foolish to install this bathroom item.
explanation.walkthrough: The contraction 'It’d be' looks like idle chatter but supplies all five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A low basin for washing oneself, installed in bathrooms beside the toilet, is a sanitary fitting of this kind.

clue.text: Riverbank robber

definitions.meaning: first meaning comes from its front half, River: the waterway flowing through Glasgow in Scotland
second meaning: half of a notorious 1930s American outlaw couple, the partner of Bonnie Parker

explanation.walkthrough: 'Riverbank' looks like one word for a waterside, but it splits into River and bank robber, the two meanings overlapping on 'bank'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scotland's great waterway through Glasgow shares a name with the outlaw of the Bonnie and Clyde gang.

clue.text: Yearn to get a jolly law member?

parts.note: to long is to yearn
taken as written
a jolly is old naval slang for a Royal Marine, RM

explanation.surface: Someone longs to become a cheerful lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jolly' looks like an adjective but is a noun: Royal Marines are nicknamed jollies. 'member' is a limb, from the phrase 'the long arm of the law'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom about the reach of the law calls its power a limb, so a body part belonging to justice.

clue.text: Certain to return tackling one or other wrong

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the letters run the other way
a tackler wraps round an opponent, so one piece grips another

parts.note: sure means certain

indicators.note: other means different, so the letters are made into a different arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Being sure of returning to take on one opponent or another is a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one or other' reads as a stock phrase, but 'other' is the signal acting on the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mistaken or incorrect is described by this formal adjective, a direct synonym for being in error.

clue.text: In part of month, egocentrics get busy

indicators.note: the answer sits in a part of the following words, as a run inside them

parts.note: read straight through, skipping the comma

explanation.surface: For part of each month, self-absorbed people get very active.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part of month' suggests a week or date, but it means some of the letters of 'month, egocentrics'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone constantly active and rushing about is described by this idiom, the same as being occupied or hectic.

clue.text: US keeping Iran struggling at first may prevent its enrichment?

definitions.text: US keeping Iran struggling at first may prevent its enrichment?

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece holds another inside
something struggling is thrashing about, so its letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: read as U's, the plural of the letter U: two of them
taken as written

indicators.note: at first means at the very start, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: America holding back a troubled Iran may stop it enriching its nuclear fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US' looks like the United States, but it is read as U's, two letter Us, which hold the rearranged IRAN. The whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The radioactive metal used as nuclear fuel is what gets enriched, so the whole sentence pictures sanctions on that element.

clue.text: Intelligence and success are trendy

parts.note: wit is quick intelligence
a hit is a success

explanation.surface: Being clever and successful makes you fashionable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' simply joins the two parts; the two-word answer splits differently from the pieces, as WITH IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone up to date with current fashions is described by this slightly dated idiom for being stylish.

clue.text: Taking a back seat during war

definitions.note: a verb phrase defining a noun: the state of doing nothing

parts.note: in means during, as in 'in the night'
action is fighting in battle

explanation.surface: Someone avoids the front line and stays out of the fighting in wartime.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one picture of a shirker, but 'during war' is the wordplay: in action, the opposite of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Staying passive and leaving others to act is the idiom's meaning, which describes a state of idleness.

clue.text: Male host enters perfectly

definitions.note: an adjective defining a noun: a male cat

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: to a T means perfectly
an MC, master of ceremonies, hosts an event

explanation.surface: A man hosting an event makes a flawless entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Male host' reads as one phrase, but the definition is the single word 'Male' and the answer is the male of a cat.
explanation.definitionFit: The word for a male feline is the defined animal, so the bare sex word stands for the creature itself.

clue.text: Dish out right measure

parts.note: to mete out is to dish out
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Serve out the correct portion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dish out right' reads as fair serving; the phrasal verb gives METE and right gives the final R.
explanation.definitionFit: A gauge that records quantities of gas or electricity is an instrument used to measure things, so the noun fits.

clue.text: Model husband claimed regularly to make cheese

indicators.note: to model is to shape or form, so the letters are moulded into a new shape

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of the word

explanation.surface: A man claimed to be the perfect spouse in order to make cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model husband' wants to be an ideal partner; 'Model' is a verb telling you to reshape the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft, blue-veined Danish dairy product is a well-known variety, so it is an example of the food named.

clue.text: Potential riot from this musical composition

indicators.note: potential means what could become something, so these letters could be rebuilt into another word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A piece of music so provocative it might start a riot.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls premieres that caused uproar; 'Potential riot' is the four letters waiting to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece written for three players or voices is one kind of musical work, so the name of the form fits.

clue.text: From policeman, a temporary discharge

indicators.note: taken from the words that follow, the letters come out of their run

parts.note: read straight through the three words

explanation.surface: A police officer is given a temporary discharge from duty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'temporary discharge' suggests leave from the force, but 'discharge' alone is the definition, used as a verb meaning issue forth.
explanation.definitionFit: To flow out or issue from a source, as light or gas does, is to give off or send out.

clue.text: Heavyweight sent back bum for not having a special suit

indicators.note: something sent back goes in the opposite direction, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: a ton is a very heavy weight
the rump is the backside

explanation.surface: A heavyweight boxer is sent home for turning up without the special costume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bum' is British slang for the backside here, not an American layabout. The answer is a bridge term.
explanation.definitionFit: In bridge, a contract played with no suit ranking above the others has no trumps, the privileged suit.
